messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel had built a life around language, ritual, and the steady rhythm of synagogue days, but at 63 he still found himself returning in his mind to the years when he was a refugee and the world had taught him that safety could vanish in a matter of seconds. He had fled as a young man from an armed crackdown, moving through checkpoints and crowded stations where shouting meant danger and the flash of a weapon could change a room instantly. He remembered the humiliation of being grabbed from behind in a crush at a border crossing, unprepared hands on his shoulders while men yelled and rifles were raised, and he had never quite shaken the sense that his body had been made for alarm. Even now, if someone touched him without warning in the hallway of the synagogue or at a crowded Shabbat table, he would jolt and go rigid before he could think. A raised voice in a meeting, even when it was only someone’s excitement, could pull him back to the old fear so sharply that he would lose his place mid-sentence. When he saw a police officer’s holster, a hunting knife at a family gathering, or even a tool that looked weapon-like, his attention narrowed and his chest tightened, as if the next second might be the one that mattered.

Those moments did not end with the startle itself. After an unexpected touch or the sight of something weapon-like, Daniel would immediately pull inward and begin punishing himself in private, telling himself he deserved to suffer for surviving when others had not. He would distract himself with study, prayer books, email, or paperwork, staying busy so he would not have to sit with what had been stirred up, and he had increasingly avoided emotional closeness with his partner, fearing that intimacy would expose how fragile he really was. At first these habits seemed like ways to get through the day, but they had become part of how he lived: a reflex to numb, withdraw, and deny himself comfort whenever the old fear was touched.

What Daniel believed about himself sat close to the center of his distress. He was convinced that his body had become a traitor, that it kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe in his own study or walking home from synagogue. He could feel his concentration fray during sermons, staff meetings, and even while reading Torah portions, and this made him worry that he could no longer trust himself to remain steady in the role he had spent decades occupying. He often thought that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that a braver or more capable person would not have been swept up and powerless in the same way. Those appraisals fed his sense that he was unsafe in the world and incompetent within it, and they left him scanning constantly for where to sit, choosing the edge of the room, the wall seat, the aisle seat, any place where he felt more protected. His world had narrowed to a handful of places that felt tolerable, and anywhere else felt uncertain enough that he could not relax.

The narrowing itself made the symptoms harder to escape. Because Daniel was so watchful for shouting, sudden contact, and anything that resembled a weapon, he began noticing them everywhere: a congregant calling across the room, a hand landing on his back before he had time to brace, a ceremonial object that briefly looked like a blade under bright light. Each time, his alarm spiked and he recoiled into distance or busied himself with something else, and afterward he was harsher with himself than before, which only deepened his belief that his body was unreliable and that he had failed in some basic way. That self-criticism kept the old image of himself as weak and undeserving close at hand, and it made ordinary closeness feel risky, because intimacy invited being seen in that state. Over months, he found himself sitting apart at dinners, leaving conversations early, and taking extra routes through the building to avoid crowded hallways where a careless touch might catch him off guard. His avoidance brought short-lived relief, but it also kept his world full of reminders that he was not at ease anywhere except in a few tightly controlled spots.

By the time he came for help, Daniel was exhausted by how much effort it took to keep himself composed. In his relationship he had become emotionally distant, and at work he worried that his concentration slips and constant seat-checking were beginning to show. He sought treatment because he no longer wanted to live as if danger were waiting in every room, and because the old conviction that he deserved suffering had begun to feel less like discipline and more like a prison. What frightened him most was the possibility that his body would never stop sounding the alarm, and what he hoped for, quietly but sincerely, was to trust himself enough to remain present with the people and places that still mattered to him.
